experiments.title: Who gets the drink?
experiments.hook: Swap one name and find the few parts of the model that track who's who.
experiments.prompt: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to

patching.clean: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to
patching.corrupted: When Mary and John went to the store, Mary gave a drink to

lookFor: Check Predictions first: GPT-2 small should favor " Mary", the person who didn't do the giving.
In Swap & Compare, press Run Patching. Pry copies each attention head, one at a time, from the original sentence into the swapped one and measures how much of the " Mary" answer comes back.
Most squares stay pale. A small number of heads, mostly in the later layers, carry most of the effect.

found.summary: Wang et al. traced this exact kind of sentence in GPT-2 small and described a circuit of about two dozen attention heads. Some find the repeated name, some suppress it, and a group they called "name mover" heads (in layers 9 and 10) copy the other name to the output. They also note the circuit is an incomplete explanation of the model's behavior.

citations.label: Wang et al. 2022, Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small

experiments.title: Knock out the name movers
experiments.hook: Switch off three heads the research points at and see if the model notices.
experiments.prompt: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to
lookFor: Pry has already picked heads 9.9, 9.6 and 10.0 for you in the Attention tab. Press "Run Ablated (3)" there.
Compare the normal top-5 with the ablated top-5. Does " Mary" lose ground, and by how much?
Don't be surprised if the answer survives. Big networks often have spare parts.

found.summary: In the same study, Wang et al. identified 9.9, 9.6 and 10.0 as the main name mover heads. When they knocked them out, other heads they called "backup name movers" partly took over, so the drop was smaller than you might expect. Pry switches heads off by setting their output to zero, while Wang et al. mostly replaced it with an average, so treat your numbers as a rough echo, not a replication.

citations.label: Wang et al. 2022, Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small

experiments.title: Spot the copycat heads
experiments.hook: Repeat a made-up phrase and watch the model look back to copy what came next.
experiments.prompt: Pip ordered zebra lamps from Quorn. Pip ordered zebra lamps from
lookFor: The model has never seen this phrase, so the only way to guess the last word is to look back at the first copy. Check Predictions for " Qu" (the start of Quorn).
The Attention grid is set to "Looks back (how far)". Bright squares are heads that reach far back in the sentence, not just to the previous word.
Click a bright head in the middle layers. On the second copy, its attention should point at the word just after the earlier match.

found.summary: Olsson et al. named these "induction heads": heads that find an earlier copy of the current word and attend to the word that came after it, so it can be copied forward. They found them in many models, and argue (with strongest evidence in small models) that they are an important part of how models learn from their context.

citations.label: Olsson et al. 2022, In-context Learning and Induction Heads

experiments.title: Watch it make up its mind
experiments.hook: Peek at the model's best guess after every layer, not just the last one.
experiments.prompt: The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of
lookFor: Each row is a layer. It shows what the model would say if it had to answer right there.
Early rows usually show vague or odd guesses. Find the first row where " Paris" shows up near the top.
Notice that the answer tends to settle in the later layers, not all at once at the end.

found.summary: nostalgebraist introduced this "logit lens" on GPT-2 and found its guesses often sharpen gradually toward the final answer across layers. Later work showed the plain logit lens can be misleading, especially in early layers and other models, and proposed a trained variant (the tuned lens). So read the early rows as a rough hint.

citations.label: nostalgebraist 2020, interpreting GPT: the logit lens
Belrose et al. 2023, Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens

experiments.title: Where does it keep facts?
experiments.hook: Swap the Eiffel Tower for the Colosseum and see which layers carry the city.
experiments.prompt: The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of

patching.clean: The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of
patching.corrupted: The Colosseum is located in the city of

lookFor: This one patches MLP layers (the model's "feed-forward" blocks) instead of attention heads. Press Run Patching in Swap & Compare.
Each bar shows how much of the Paris answer comes back when that one layer is copied from the Eiffel Tower sentence.
Look for which layers matter most. In GPT-2 small, the very first MLP often stands out. It's often described as acting like an extension of the word lookup.

found.summary: Meng et al. used a similar "restore one piece" trick (they called it causal tracing) on larger GPT models and found that MLP layers in the middle of the network, at the last word of the subject, played a decisive role in recalling facts. Pry patches each layer at every position at once and uses a much smaller model, so expect a blurrier picture than theirs.

citations.label: Meng et al. 2022, Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT (ROME)

experiments.title: Can it count years?
experiments.hook: "From 1732 to 17..": find the layers that know the end year must be bigger.
experiments.prompt: The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17

patching.clean: The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17
patching.corrupted: The war lasted from the year 1701 to the year 17

lookFor: Predictions should lean toward two-digit endings bigger than 32. It won't be perfect.
The swapped sentence starts in 1701, which tells the model almost nothing, because any later year fits. Press Run Patching in Swap & Compare.
Which MLP layers bring back the original answer? Watch the later layers in particular.

found.summary: Hanna et al. studied this exact setup in GPT-2 small. They found a few attention heads that move the start year to the end of the sentence, and MLP layers near the end of the network (roughly layers 8 to 11) that push up the years bigger than the start. They used the same model but a more targeted kind of patching than Pry's, so your picture may be blurrier.

citations.label: Hanna et al. 2023, How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?

experiments.title: He or she?
experiments.hook: See which parts of the model push a pronoun one way or the other.
lookFor: In Predictions, compare how likely " she" and " he" are. Then change "nurse" to "doctor" in the prompt box and press Run again.
Why (DLA) shows which layers and heads pushed directly toward the top guess. Big bars are the strongest direct pushers.
DLA only counts direct pushes on the answer. A part that helps by setting up later parts won't show up here.

found.summary: Vig et al. studied gender bias in GPT-2 with prompts like this one, using causal methods. They found the effect was concentrated in a small part of the network, such as a handful of attention heads. The trick behind the Why tab, splitting the answer into each part's direct contribution, comes from Elhage et al.'s framework for reading transformers.

citations.label: Vig et al. 2020, Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
Elhage et al. 2021, A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits

experiments.title: Turn up a concept
experiments.hook: Find a learned concept inside the model, then dial it up and see what it writes.
experiments.prompt: On our trip we walked along the beach and watched the ocean
lookFor: The Features tab lists concepts that were active on each word. Click " ocean" or " beach" in the token strip and read the labels.
Labels are best guesses written from examples. Some fit nicely, some are puzzling.
Then open Steering, pick one of those features, turn it up, and run. Does the continuation drift toward that concept?

found.summary: Bricken et al. showed that a sparse autoencoder can split a model's activity into many "features", many of which match a single human-readable idea. Templeton et al. scaled this up to a production model and showed that turning a feature up can steer what the model says (their "Golden Gate Bridge" demo). The features in Pry come from openly released sparse autoencoders for GPT-2 small, not from those papers.
